chunks: Ali ibn Hatim said: Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, from Abu Abdillah al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan al-Hasani, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Hamdani

The narrations differed regarding al-Fitrah (Zakat al-Fitr), so I wrote to Abu al-Hasan, the Master of the Camp (peace be upon him), asking him about that. He wrote: Al-Fitrah is one Sa' of the staple food of your land. For the people of Mecca, Yemen, Ta'if, the outskirts of Syria, Yamamah, Bahrain, the two Iraqs, Persia, Ahwaz, and Kerman, it is dates. For the central regions of Syria, it is raisins. For the people of Jazira, Mosul, and all the mountains, it is wheat or barley. For the people of Tabaristan, it is rice. For the people of Khorasan, it is wheat, except for the people of Merv and Rayy, for whom it is raisins. For the people of Egypt, it is wheat. And for those other than these, it is whatever staple food predominates for them. For the Bedouins who dwell in the deserts, it is Qit (dried yogurt). Al-Fitrah is obligatory upon you and upon all people, and upon every male or female, young or old, free or slave, weaned or infant, whom you provide for. You pay it by weight: six Artals, where the Rital of Medina is one hundred and ninety-five dirhams. Thus, the total value of Al-Fitrah is one thousand and seventy dirhams.

key_terms.الْفِطْرَة: Zakat al-Fitr, the alms-giving required at the end of Ramadan
key_terms.رِطْل: Rital, a unit of weight used in Medina
key_terms.صَاع: A traditional unit of volume measurement
key_terms.قُوت: Staple food or primary sustenance of a region

ai.seo_question: What is the specific amount and type of food required for Zakat al-Fitr in different regions according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani’s chain in al-Istibsar illustrates the Shia scholarly principle of 'customary staple' (qurot al-balad), where Zakat al-Fitr is tied to local dietary norms rather than a single universal food. It provides a detailed geographical taxonomy, assigning dates to Mecca, raisins to central Syria, and wheat or barley to Iraq and Persia, while emphasizing that the obligation extends to all dependents regardless of age or status. The text concludes with precise metrological standards, defining the weight as six Artals (equivalent to 1,170 dirhams in weight) to ensure uniformity in distribution.
